lead: A class diagram is the static picture of an object-oriented system. It lists the classes, the data each class holds (attributes), the operations it offers, and the relationships between classes. It exists so that designers, programmers and testers share one view of the data model before code is written. You use it to check multiplicity, inheritance and ownership — for example, whether one order can have many order lines, or whether an account can survive without a branch. On a phone screen, read the boxes first, then the lines.
prereq: You need 3.2 Design concepts for classes and objects, and Unit 2 for class-based requirements models.

sections.h3: The class box and the UML frame

blocks.text: UML has three building blocks: things, relationships and diagrams. A class is a thing. A line between classes is a relationship. A class diagram is one diagram made of both. The class itself is drawn as a rectangle with three compartments: name, attributes, operations.

Visibility marks sit before each member. Use + for public, − for private, # for protected and ~ for package. Underline a static member; it belongs to the class, not to one object. Write an abstract class name in italics or add {abstract}. Mark an interface with «interface» and keep its name italic.

head: Mark
Meaning
rows: public — any class can use it
private — only this class can use it
protected — this class and its subclasses
package — classes in the same package

blocks.text: Attributes usually show a type: balance: Money. Operations show parameters and a return type: deposit(amount: Money): Boolean. The diagram is static: it shows what can exist, not the order in which calls happen. Message order belongs to 3.7 interaction diagrams.

An association is a solid line between classes. A role name at an end says what that end means, such as accountHolder. Multiplicity says how many objects at one end may link to one object at the other end. Write 1, 0..1, *, 1..*, or a range such as 2..4. Read each label from the class at the far end.

head: Relationship
Symbol
rows: solid line, optional arrow for navigability
hollow triangle pointing to the parent
dashed arrow to the thing used
dashed line with hollow triangle to an interface

blocks.text: Aggregation means a part can live without its whole: a department has teachers, but a teacher still exists if the department closes. Composition means the part dies with its whole: an order line has no meaning after its order is deleted. Generalization is an is-a link; a savings account is an account. Dependency is a uses link and is weaker than association. Realization is a class promising to obey an interface.
Two exam slips are common. The hollow diamond is aggregation and the filled diamond is composition. A plain line with multiplicity is an association, not a dependency; dependency uses a dashed arrow.

sections.h3: From a paragraph to a finished diagram

items: Underline the nouns in the requirement text. Keep the nouns that the system must remember; drop synonyms, outside systems and simple attributes.
Write each class box with its name, attributes and operations. Add visibility marks. Underline static members and mark abstract classes or interfaces.
Draw each relationship. Choose association for a lasting link, aggregation or composition for whole–part, generalization for is-a, dependency for uses, and realization for implements.
Add role names and multiplicity at every end. Read each requirement sentence back against the diagram; fix any line that cannot answer how many.

blocks.text: An object diagram is a snapshot of one moment. It uses the same boxes, but object names are underlined and values are shown, such as ravi: Customer. Use it to test one example; use the class diagram to state the rules for all examples.

figure.caption: The worked example: Branch 1 .. 0..* Account, Customer 1 .. 1..* Account, and Account 1 .. 0..* Transaction. The highlighted line is composition — a transaction dies with its account — and each multiplicity is read from the class at the far end.

spec.aria: Four classes, Branch, Customer, Account and Transaction, joined by three lines: Branch to Account with multiplicity 1 .. 0..*, Customer to Account with 1 .. 1..*, and Account to Transaction with 1 .. 0..*, the last drawn as composition.

examples.question: Draw the class diagram for a bank. A customer holds one or more accounts. An account may have two or more holders when it is a joint account. A branch has many accounts. Every transaction belongs to exactly one account. (a) How many classes? (b) Give the multiplicity expressions on the relationships. Add a filled diamond if a transaction cannot exist after its account is closed.
steps: Step 1 — find the classes. The nouns to keep are Customer, Account, Branch and Transaction, so (a) gives 4 classes.

Step 2 — Customer to Account. The text says a customer holds one or more accounts, so the Account end is 1..*. Read back from Account to Customer: an account has at least one holder, so the Customer end is 1..*. Write Customer 1 .. 1..* Account. The 'two or more holders' rule holds only for joint accounts, so it cannot be a multiplicity on the whole association; add a JointAccount class, or attach a constraint such as {joint accounts have 2..* holders}.
Step 3 — Branch to Account. One branch has 0..* accounts; one account belongs to 1 branch. Write Branch 1 .. 0..* Account.
Step 4 — Account to Transaction. One account has 0..* transactions over its life; one transaction belongs to 1 account. Write Account 1 .. 0..* Transaction.
Step 5 — ownership. A transaction cannot exist after its account is closed, so add a filled diamond at the Account end of Account–Transaction: composition.

Step 6 — draw the four boxes with attributes such as Customer.customerId, Account.balance, Branch.branchCode and Transaction.txnId. The three multiplicity expressions are Customer 1 .. 1..* Account, Branch 1 .. 0..* Account, and Account 1 .. 0..* Transaction.
examples.answer: There are 4 classes — Customer, Account, Branch and Transaction; the multiplicities are Customer 1 .. 1..* Account, Branch 1 .. 0..* Account, and Account 1 .. 0..* Transaction, with a filled diamond on Account–Transaction for composition.

traps: A class diagram never shows time or message order. If your arrows carry a fixed sequence, you have drawn a sequence diagram, not a class diagram.
The hollow diamond is aggregation; the filled diamond is composition. A composition part dies with its whole.
Multiplicity is read at the far end. A line marked 1 .. 0..* means one object at this end links to zero or more at the other end; it does not mean the class has at most one object.
An abstract class and an interface are not the same. Both may have operations, but an interface has no state and is marked «interface».
Not every noun is a class. A name or amount that is stored inside one class is an attribute, not a separate box.

quiz.q: What are the three compartments of a UML class box?
Explain the difference between aggregation and composition with one example each.
quiz.a: Aggregation is a weak whole–part link: the part can exist alone, such as a department and its teachers. Composition is a strong whole–part link: the part dies with the whole, such as an order and its order lines.

quiz.q: A joint bank account needs at least two holders. Write the multiplicity on the Account end of the Customer–Account association.
quiz.a: Account end: 1..* (0..* if a customer need not hold an account). The Customer end is 1..*; the 'at least two holders' rule appears there only as a constraint on joint accounts, not as a blanket 2..*.

quiz.q: A line reads Order 1 — 0..* OrderLine. What does each label mean, and why is a filled diamond appropriate here?
quiz.a: One order has zero or more order lines; each order line belongs to exactly one order. The filled diamond shows composition because an order line has no meaning after its order is deleted.

quiz.q: Give the meaning of the visibility marks +, −, # and ~.
A class SmsAlert implements an interface Notifier. Which UML relationship connects them, and what symbol is used?
quiz.a: Realization, drawn as a dashed line with a hollow triangle pointing to Notifier; SmsAlert is the implementing class.

quiz.q: Why is a class diagram a poor place to show the steps of a UPI payment? Which diagram should be used?
quiz.a: A class diagram is static: it shows classes and their links, not the order of messages over time. Use a sequence diagram or a communication diagram (called a collaboration diagram in older UML) from 3.7 to show the payment steps.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, class diagrams feed code generation, database object-relational mappings, and API schemas. Tools such as PlantUML and Mermaid let a team keep diagrams in version control beside the code. UML also provides association classes and qualified associations for links that carry their own data. Search for those terms, and for the Object Constraint Language (OCL), which writes rules that a line and a multiplicity cannot express.
